reviews.review: I have to give credit to [b]Hacknet[/b] when it comes to [b]originality[/b] in a overloaded [i]simulator[/i] world. Barring the [b]stench of [i]anti-political-correctness-gamer[/i]-like logs[/b] - thank god they are optional to read - and [b]how foreign the commands feel at times[/b] despite the tutorial and help pages, [b]Hacknet[/b] is [b]super fun[/b] once you get a general grasp of what you are [i]actually[/i] doing. Although [b]the majority of missions[/b] in the game [i]may[/i] seem [b]inane[/b], the [b]main storyline and [i]a few[/i] of the anonymous requests[/b] do provide the player with a [b]sense of purpose[/b] and a [b]genuine feeling that what they are doing [i]matters[/i][/b]. Sadly, it does [b][i]not[/i][/b] do a great job at [b]educating people who [i]might[/i] be unfamiliar with coding language[/b], and it certainly does not make an effort to explain certain processes in laymen terms. On top of that, the [b]localization is a disaster[/b], so I would [b][i]strongly[/i] suggest[/b] potential players to [b]stick to the English version[/b]. However, overall, [b]Hacknet[/b] is a [b]damn entertaining[/b] [i]simulation[/i] game and a [b]fresh take on the genre[/b] that [i]may[/i] pleasantly surprise you.

Hacknet is an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator and that kind of computer games have been around a lot... but Hacknet has some differences that make the game special. The graphics are very modern and bring the hacker feeling first class to the player so that you really feel like being in the setting. You can also play the game with the mouse and click on the individual tasks, but with the text console you are much faster and it creates an even better game realism. Anyway, if you program it yourself and know how to solve problems with the CLI. The story is as well as with EXAPUNKS rather conspiratorial and you are addressed by a person via mail. This person already seems to be dead and now you have to explore these backgrounds. Hacknet mixes computer games and reality pretty well, because if you move through other file systems, delete log files and old chat processes or read mails and have to deal with the individual ports again and again, you can quickly forget the time around you. The levels and commands are really different, get data, delete data or break into a certain server. There is quite a lot and Hacknet is very well worked out in terms of content. This game has also been developed for a certain target group and you should be interested in information technology.
Lots of little odds and ends and pathways, if you want to explore it all.

Fantastic game. Beat it a while ago, but I figured I'd write a review anyway

Graphics are on point. It was very easy to get used to the interface, but I remember being a bit overwhelmed at the start. The semi-tutorial takes you through the process of the gameplay very nicely, so it's an overall smooth start.

The gameplay is fantastic. It does get a bit stale at one point in the game, and it gets a bit cryptic in some task descriptions, so I admit to having to look up a walkthrough every now and then. The puzzles are quite a lot of fun, and don't feel very repetitive, even if you get used to the generally pretty generic rhythm of the game.

There's a bit of missing suspense and a lack of clear enemies makes it a bit difficult to feel pressure when playing the game, but every now and then, a timer comes up, and it gets very dramatic, which elevates the gameplay a bit.

I loved playing it despite the small flaws. The gameplay is suprisingly riveting despite what might seem like a very simplistic set of controls. There are also tons of easter eggs hidden in the files you hack into, and reading them kinda relieves the seriousness of the game a bit, and makes room for some comedic moments
Solid puzzle game if you like this theme.

Hacknet is the most satisfying hacking game I've ever played. I admire the overall design of the game which nicely balances quite complex hacking subjects with casual approach for less advanced players, in a result striking at the sweet spot of a satisfying, complex, yet approachable gameplay.

The best part of Hacknet is definitely its puzzles, which start from very simple and get progressively harder, but nothing extreme enough. The story is alright for what the game is based upon and I must admit that it's one of the best puzzle games you can play today. I can happily recommend this title to everybody looking for a good hacking-oriented puzzle game, especially to those people that do not aim for complex mechanics and technical details or real knowledge, but rather something more approachable for a causal gamer, while still not cutting on the content that more advanced players can enjoy on their own.

I'm very happy that I gave Hacknet a try and managed to finish it.

---

If you liked my review, you can find more of them on [b][url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/ArchiPL/recommended/]my profile[/url][/b] and on my [b][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/10639590/]curator page[/url][/b].

Hacknet is NOT a simulator, but rather an impressively addictive puzzle game which introduces the player to simplifications of real-world concepts in such a way that they feel as if they are easily able to become the world's greatest hacker. There are some secret avenues and plot twists that reward those who dig a little deeper, which is also neat. The humor is absolutely top notch and had me actually laugh out loud in several places. Kudos!

As for the downsides, the music is generally rather bland, the faux-early-2010's internet vernacular is understandably dated and can be a bit cringy, although it's not terrible, and finally, the puzzles and interface can be a little bit bizarre at times - ironically more fiddly than real life security consultancy and penetration.

All-in-all, a nifty game on sale, for around $5, although I'd be hard pressed to recommend it to the average non-puzzle gamer for more.

A great game with an extremely fun and innovative take on the "ARG" theme surrounding hacking - This was recommended to me by a friend, and I'm happy to have trusted their judgement on that one.

Gameplay wise, it offers a unique mode of interaction, of which most can be done via typing only in an in-game console. Meanwhile, the majority of the game also offers a UI for the less... experienced or "nerdy" of us. Both methods of interaction are integrated flawlessly to provide the player with a really fun new way to play through the game, while still allowing for navigating with a mouse pointer.

The game has a story line and some "jobs" you can take in-between the main storyline, but everything is surprisingly open world when it comes to what you want to do, and when. If you have the correct tools available to you, you can potentially explore lot of "areas" and content that you don't necessarily need to access during the jobs and main story. At any point in the game, you can dig around a computer or server, find and decypher files, recover logs, emails, etc, and learn more about groups and people and what they do in the safety of their privacy.

I highly recommend at least trying it out, as the unique gameplay alone is worth experiencing.

The description is somewhat misleading, particularly this excerpt:

[quote=Fellow Traveller]Hacknet is an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator for PC.[/quote]

Let me be clear by saying that this is not a true-to-life hacking simulator which will help you grasp real-world skills in computer hacking.  What you'll receive if you purchase this title (and I highly recommend that you do) is a text-based puzzle game with a computer hacking theme.  To be honest, common sense should tell you that Steam wouldn't even allow, what would essentially be, a hacker training programme on their platform.

If you are in the market to attempt real computer hacking, nothing is stopping you from following a guide on YouTube to set up your own server and then breach its security.  Just don't then make someone else's server your next target!

That being said, if you enjoy or are fascinated by Command-line Interfaces, have an interest in computing or just enjoy fast-paced puzzle games with a gripping story, pick up this title.

Full disclosure: I am a giant nerd. Grew up more on computers (and dogs!) than, like, ya know.... PEOPLE... The point is, if you put a terminal or a shell in front of me I get super excited and it's instantly, like, +5,000 to appreciation for thing.

ANYWAY.

This game is sublime. I think, oftentimes, if you look up hacking sims, you get to get stuff like Uplink, which is very good, certainly, and I DO recommend it, but Hacknet was made as a spiritual successor to it (by the dev's own confirmation), and I consider it better in every way. Uplink is a little more sandbox-y (think, like, a game that is entirely a radiant quest from Skyrim. Except, like... good. And dynamic); Hacknet actually has a story. There are a number of missions to do, and it's not linear in the sense that you have to do everything in order, but there are a couple factions you can go with and you'll get different tasks from them. It all culminates in the same storyline at the end, but I don't mean that as a negative. The writing is really good, the gameplay is engaging, and there are tons of little incidentals you can find for worldbuilding and extraneous fun (IRC logs are a really good example of this, and many of those are extremely well-observed; tech-heads, I can guarantee, will find some gems in there).

Essentially, you encounter external systems and learn to crack them. For various reasons. Everything from "delete this sensitive file" to "modify a file's contents" to "find out where this signal came from" to "cripple this server" and others. And that's just for starters. Eventually you start dealing with conspiracies, and your missions get really involved, having to crack multiple terminals, finding links between them, worming your way into other systems, finding user credentials, reading e-mails, finding synched external devices, etc, etc. You have to break through security before you can CRACK the system, naturally, and different systems have different layers requiring different programs to surpass. It's almost entirely SKiddying, for those of you who are also dorks like myself, but it's very entertainingly-done and the graphics built to illustrate Computer Happenings (R)(C) are really rad. I wouldn't be surprised if you needed a guide at some point, your first time through, but, well, put it this way: collaboration between agents is pretty common, so don't feel bad.

The interface is really cool, you CAN do just about everything with the mouse, if you're wired that way, but you can also use the console, which is my preferred way of doing things. There are multiple .sys overlays you can enable, as well, to change your GUI and layout, which adds a little customization (some of them done by commissioned artist). The expansion that's since come out is a lot of fun, and adds probably another four to six hours to a game that I'd say is around ten hours your first time through, if you know what you're doing. Decently replayable, too.

Finally, I will say that this is one of my favorite soundtracks I've ever heard. I've never seen a game before this that uses Vaporwave as its backing, but it makes a lot of sense; that's a really good genre for focus-demanding work, like this game presents. Also, they used HOME on the soundtrack, and they are one of my absolute favorites (shill, shill). I will also say, while the OST is extremely chill, they DO use one of the higher-octane tracks from Hotline Miami 2, and I daresay it fits even better here.

All in all, you can get the game, its expansion, and both OSTs for twenty bucks, when it ISN'T on sale, and I find that to be a friggin' steal. On a closing note, there's no other game that will actually get your adrenaline pumping entering text commands at a shell. I defy anyone who says they can do the endgame of the original or Labyrinths without a significant spike in vitals.
